channel.title: World Barbecue Report
channel.description: A weekly reading of the world of barbecue by the International Outdoor Barbecue Sports Federation (IOBSF). Free to republish with credit to IOBSF and a link to iobsf.org.

item.title: World Barbecue Report, Inaugural Issue (Third Week of November 2026)
item.description:
Competition barbecue: At the 37th Jack Daniel's World Championship Invitational Barbecue in Lynchburg, Tennessee, the Smellaque team led by Janice Smella of Calgary, Canada, took first place. It was her third attempt. That a team from across the border has stood at the top of the contest known as the holy ground of the American South shows that competition barbecue is already moving beyond a single nation's tradition toward an international sport.
The World Food Championships, held in Indianapolis from 15 to 18 October, drew more than 400 teams from over 35 states and 14 countries, with total prize money above 400,000 dollars. Jordan Davis of Carmel, Indiana, won the barbecue category, and Adi Melkman of Utrecht, the Netherlands, won the live fire category. The burger title went to Tatewaki Takano of Tokyo, Japan. European and Asian names at the top of the fire categories mark the passage of this contest from an American festival to a sport shared by the world. The ten category champions will compete for the final title at the Final Table in spring 2027.
Developing talent: In Texas, high school barbecue teams continue to compete for places at the state championship. Teams from Temple High and Copperas Cove announced their qualification on 13 November. When schools teach the craft of the fire in the language of formal competition, it is the most concrete evidence that the Pro Barbecuer can be raised within an educational system.
Barbecue industry: Traeger, the leading pellet grill maker, reported its third-quarter results on 4 November. Total revenue fell 40.4% to 74.7 million dollars, and grill revenue fell 48.1% to 39.7 million dollars. Management expects revenue to grow again in the fourth quarter, helped by shipments shifted from the third quarter and its expansion at Lowe's. As the equipment demand that piled up in backyards during the pandemic recedes, the industry has entered a phase in which it must think less about selling more machines and more about renewing the reasons to light a fire.
Asia: China's barbecue market is growing and consolidating at the same time. According to the Hongcan Industry Research Institute (红餐产业研究院), the Chinese barbecue (烧烤) market reached 268 billion yuan in 2025, up 4.3%, and is expected to exceed 280 billion yuan in 2026. Yet the number of outlets fell to 409,000 as of February 2026. China is a major production base for the world's barbecue equipment, with industrial clusters in Guangdong and Henan. This explains why AOBE 2027 in Guangzhou next May is held at the heart of the equipment industry.
In Korea, the autumn festivals continued. The 2026 Hongseong Global Barbecue Festival, held around Hongjuseong from 29 October to 1 November, offered discounted Hanwoo beef and Korean pork and self-service charcoal grilling. At the Jinan Highland Kimchi Bossam Festival, black pork barbecue also took centre stage among local foods. If Korean barbecue festivals still lean toward promoting meat consumption, the next step will be a move toward Sports Barbecue with competition and ritual.
Around the world: An asador contest in La Pampa, Argentina, a charity braai competition in South Africa, a churrasco festival in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and a gastronomy festival in French Guadeloupe followed one another last week. The names differ, yet the way they gather people before the fire is the same.
Research: A study published in PLOS One in June this year confirmed traces of repeated fire use in deposits dated between about 1.07 and 1.79 million years ago at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa. The researchers identified these traces through luminescence, in which burned bone glows red under blue light. They added, however, that these bones alone cannot establish that early humans cooked routinely. Archaeological dating has moved one step closer to the view that finds the origin of cooking with fire in Homo erectus.
